# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
> — Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial*, 3rd ed. (1996) [@Simon1996SciencesArtificial, p. 111]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Herbert Simon defined design as charting the course from our present situation to a preferred one. This places problem choice, abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs at the core of our technical work. While automation contributes substantially to this journey, our primary architectural contribution lies in shaping that course into a coherent system, establishing exactly what the evidence supports, and making any residual risk fully transparent.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
If a capable AI-assisted design system can formulate studies, generate artifacts, search design spaces, run tools, interpret failures, and recommend a design, what core technical work do we as architects still contribute?
:::

We assume a capable AI-assisted system can shoulder substantial workloads by executing everything from initial study formulation through final technical recommendation. This includes coordinating specialized methodologies, driving verification tools, and managing failure-driven revisions across our most exhaustive design studies. Nothing in our discussion relies on clinging to a protected set of tasks that only human engineers can execute.

Our role as architects is not simply to mop up whatever tasks automation fails to absorb. The essential difficulty of software engineering lies in rigorously specifying the system rather than merely representing it [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]. Similarly, our fundamental technical contribution rests on *cross-layer architect ownership*, defined as the ultimate responsibility of the architect to frame system problems across all 8 layers of the prompt stack, establish abstraction boundaries, synthesize cross-domain tradeoffs across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers, and declare residual risk rather than delegating technical accountability to automated tools or isolated domain specialists. We choose the right abstractions and delineate the critical system boundaries across our host RV64GCV vector-capable CPU cores, dedicated NPU tensor accelerator engines, Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler passes, SRAM/LPDDR5 memory hierarchies, AMBA AXI5 interconnects, and 2.5D Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) packaging links under a 3\ W TDP target in TSMC N7 or 3\ nm-class LP mobile process nodes. We synthesize these diverse components into a cohesive and feasible design. We interpret conflicting results, hunt down missing evidence, and declare exactly which uncertainties remain. Ultimately, we actively shape both the architecture of the system and the design process we use to build it.

Because organizational assignments vary across projects, one person might wear multiple hats, tempting us to blur the lines between four distinct pillars of engineering work. First, the *domain specialist* qualifies results within a focused discipline and owns any technical signoffs. Second, the *architect* integrates those isolated results into a unified system vision and declares exactly which uncertainties remain. Third, the *commitment authority* decides whether our proposed design actually advances to the next phase. Finally, the *accountable organization* provisions resources for these roles and owns the real-world consequences of the final product.

Within this framework, our distinctive output as architects is a fully supported architecture recommendation. We must explicitly define the design under consideration, document the evidence that validates it, expose any lingering risks, and establish the exact triggers that would force a review. Our domain specialists push qualified results upward for system-level synthesis. We push reframed questions and demands for rigorous stress tests back down. Our commitment authority receives this deliberate recommendation, preventing them from stumbling into a decision by mere implication (@fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment).

![**Technical synthesis precedes commitment.** Our domain specialists qualify scoped results and checks across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers. We (the architects) frame the problem, choose the proper abstractions and system boundaries, connect the physical and logical layers, interpret disagreements, and declare the residual risk before presenting a supported technical recommendation. A separate commitment authority then advances, holds, or rejects our design. Our accountable organization resources these distinct roles, and changed operational conditions can trigger us to reopen the technical work.](images/F11-architecture-synthesis-commitment){#fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment width="100%" fig-alt="An accountable organization surrounds three distinct roles. Domain specialists qualify scoped results, checks, artifacts, and failures. We, the architects, frame the problem, choose our abstractions and system boundaries, connect layers, interpret disagreements, state residual risk, and retain access to decisive artifacts and failures. Our supported technical recommendation then reaches a separate commitment authority that advances, holds, or rejects the design. Continuous monitoring and changed conditions return to the architect and may reopen specialist work."}

This operational separation is not a rigid one-way approval chain. A failed verification check might force us to reframe the architecture problem or demand new observational data. Additionally, late-stage shifts in target workloads, software stacks, EDA tools, manufacturing processes, or deployed environments can invalidate our recommendation's foundational assumptions. A management commitment decision does not override the technical results that preceded it. Table @tbl-architect-technical-judgments outlines the recurring judgments we make to forge isolated specialist results into one product recommendation.

We look to NASA's systems engineering guidance as a precedent for this structural separation. Their decision analysis framework produces analytical comparisons and formal recommendations for a distinct decision-making authority [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, sec. 6.8 and app. B]. This precedent validates our distinction between raw technical analysis and authorized product decisions.

Every individual IP block or subsystem can operate in isolation yet fail to yield a functioning product when integrated. A host CPU core might clear timing closure. An NPU accelerator might hit its target TFLOPS/Watt. An LPDDR5 memory controller might validate read/write queues. A UCIe PHY might achieve clean eye diagrams. As architects, it is our responsibility to verify whether these victories describe a single viable product operating under a globally consistent set of workload, software, interface, memory, power, packaging, thermal, and business assumptions.

Locally qualified victories are insufficient to support a system recommendation. We must step in to frame the overarching problem, choose the proper abstractions and component boundaries, integrate the stack across physical and logical layers, and arbitrate disciplinary disagreements. This synthesis produces our technical recommendation. It insulates the raw specialist data from the overarching program claims and the final business decision to advance. The precision and scope of our supporting evidence establish limits on what we can present for commitment and dictate which future disruptions will mandate a reopening of our technical review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we master five core architectural competencies.

- Distinguish architecture recommendations from specialist results, program claims, and organizational commitments.
- Frame coherent architecture problems that maintain integrity across workloads, boundaries, and interventions.
- Select abstractions, components, and checks tailored to the technical problem.
- Integrate cross-disciplinary specialist results across CPU cores, NPUs, memory, and packaging into a unified system design.
- Interpret conflicting evidence, state bounded recommendations, and identify triggers for review.
:::

## Delegating Without Losing Technical Contact {#sec-delegating-without-losing-contact}

As computer architects, four conditions govern how we assign design work. We must be able to observe the candidate state, reverse a proposed change, reject a bad result through independent checks, and bound the cross-layer consequences. A bounded array mapping sweep or a focused tool run often satisfies these conditions, allowing us to hand off the work to an automated method or domain specialist.

Freezing a software-facing interface or a die-to-die interconnect configuration presents an entirely different challenge. Freezing an instruction set architecture (ISA) contract between the host CPU and an NPU or fixing the PHY lane count on a 2.5D UCIe chiplet packaging link constitutes a difficult-to-reverse cross-layer decision. It hardens assumptions across compiler and runtime behavior, memory hierarchies, RTL, physical implementation, thermal dissipation, and product integration. In such cases, we must reconcile that evidence, empowering the commitment authority to decide whether the transition proceeds. Both scenarios demand that our team remains competent enough to challenge underlying assumptions and trace failures beyond the delegated boundary.

This assignment rule ensures our core architecture judgments remain connected as work flows between people and tools. As architects, we formulate the system question. We choose our representations alongside their omissions. We select the methods and environments. We mandate independent checks. We integrate cross-layer results. Ultimately, we determine what our combined engineering efforts support.

These judgments must remain a central part of our engineering practice because a computer architecture is never simply the union of locally successful component outputs. It represents a deliberate choice of mechanisms and interfaces designed to work under the conditions our product will encounter in the real world. We must inspect disagreements, ferret out exceptions, and probe the limits of our models before determining which residual uncertainties our next design transition can carry forward.

This premise changes how we maintain technical contact with our designs. When we look at historical shifts in abstraction [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel], we see that our discipline delegated lower-level tasks because we preserved technical contact through diagnostic capabilities. We must retain our ability to challenge a formulation, inspect decisive artifacts and failures, trace results across complex interfaces, and recognize when a model or check is being pushed outside its support. If we fail to do so, our delegation will erode the competence we need to judge the designs we produce.

We draw a parallel from human factors research. It distinguishes misuse (when people rely on automation inappropriately) from disuse (when they neglect its capabilities entirely) [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. This distinction explains why our direct technical contact must survive any task delegation. It does not dictate which specific architecture decisions a human expert or an automated system should control.

As more local work becomes delegable, our technical role shifts upstream toward choosing the right problems and abstractions. We shift across the system toward defining rigorous interfaces and checks. We shift downstream toward interpreting uncertainty and formulating recommendations. This shift does not lift us above the engineering details. We must retain enough hands-on contact with our artifacts, our tools, and our system failure modes to intervene the moment an abstraction breaks or whenever the empirical evidence no longer supports our design decisions.

## Framing Cross-Layer Problems {#sec-framing-architecture-problem}

We do not wait for a search to finish before stepping in. As architects, our work begins before the candidate set exists, and we remain involved after a local result looks clean. Our technical contribution lies in deciding what the system is, which cross-layer relationships matter, and which consequences our studies must expose. We create or refine the mechanisms, interfaces, abstractions, and fallback options that bind specialist results into a single system. Recognizing that advances in compiler technology shifted the hardware-software boundary is what enabled the RISC approach [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. The architecture question remains: Do these pieces form a feasible system that meets our product obligations?

Beyond defining the system, we must design the workflows that drive these decisions. We determine which methods propose changes, which modeling tools measure relevant properties, which validation checks gate candidates, and which roles resolve disagreements. Ultimately, these methodological choices define what our studies can observe and which architectural conclusions they can support.

Consider the initial Lighthouse prompt. It states an ambition, but an ambition is not a well-posed architecture problem. A directive like *"Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload"* leaves variables open. It ignores the choice of representative workloads, the supported software stack, the product boundary, alternative design points, operating conditions, tradeoffs, and the specific decisions we need to make. We must frame the ambition across all 8 layers of the Lighthouse Prompt Stack. We transform it into a challengeable architecture question that anchors the following design layers.

1. **Workload.** Real-time spatial tracking and neural rendering tasks from XRBench, CPU application benchmarks from SPEC2026, and mobile inference suites from MLPerf.
2. **ISA & ABI contract.** An RV64GCV 64-bit application processor core equipped with 128-bit vector extensions adhering to standard ABI conventions.
3. **Compute organization.** A heterogeneous SoC block uniting the RV64GCV vector-capable CPU core with a dedicated NPU tensor accelerator engine.
4. **Memory & data movement.** A multi-level cache hierarchy (32\ KB L1, 512\ KB L2, 4\ MB L3) and TCM scratchpads linked via AMBA AXI5 and UCIe chiplet interconnects, optimizing interconnect energy per bit.
5. **Power envelope.** A 3\ W sustained Thermal Design Power (TDP) target in a passive optical frame form factor.
6. **Compiler / runtime stack.** Triton kernel fusion, LLVM vector code generation, and MLIR lowering passes.
7. **Physical constraints.** TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class LP mobile process node floorplanning, wire delays, DRCs, and routing congestion.
8. **Reliability & verification.** Red-teaming agent verification, LLM-as-a-Judge confirmation bias mitigation, IP indemnification legal risk audits, and NRE tapeout ROI gatekeeping.

Once we frame the problem across these 8 layers, we dictate what our design systems must contain. If we are studying array utilization, our environment might need a cycle-level model and a mapping search. However, if we are making a hard decision about freezing that array alongside its software-facing interface and UCIe packaging link, we must expose a broader reality. We need instruments that capture Triton, LLVM, and MLIR compiler behavior, memory traffic, UCIe PHY latency, physical implementation feasibility, total 3\ W subsystem power, IP indemnification, and the consequences of future modifications. It is our architecture question that drives the necessary abstractions, never the other way around.

We rely on a set of core architecture judgments, summarized in @tbl-architect-technical-judgments, to transform isolated results into a cohesive product recommendation. While we might distribute these individual judgments across different subsystems, properties, or design transitions, our architecture team must verify whether these fragmented domain claims assemble into one feasible system.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one our product needs solved? | Our task is not merely to maximize NPU array utilization. We must decide whether an implementation-facing RV64GCV CPU to NPU interface, Triton/LLVM/MLIR lowering, and memory hierarchy meet our 3\ W mobile XR obligation. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can we simplify for this decision? | A cycle-level NPU model can compare matrix mappings locally, but it cannot hide Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler lowering, SRAM/LPDDR5 memory traffic, UCIe interconnect energy, physical timing, or our 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | We cannot separate NPU array dimensions and dataflow from host RV64GCV vector core task dispatch, UCIe chiplet interconnects, memory bandwidth, thermal dissipation, DRCs, and the physical implementation path they require. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do our mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, and implementation choices form one feasible system? | Our NPU array, RV64GCV CPU contract, compiler passes, LPDDR5 memory path, 3\ W thermal constraint, UCIe die-to-die PHY, and firmware fallback behavior must form one implementable subsystem rather than separate local wins. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has our formulation, representation, or tool path left out? | XRBench, SPEC2026, and MLPerf workloads, software interface cost, 3\ W TDP subsystem power, UCIe signal integrity, physical timing closure, IP indemnification, NRE tapeout ROI, and hardware containment remain open obligations. |
| **Cross-layer tradeoff** | Which feasible point best serves our product when objectives conflict? | We must compose RV64GCV tail latency, NPU matrix throughput, LPDDR5 interconnect power, UCIe chiplet routing, and review burden rather than delegating them to separate optimizers. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does our proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | Our directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor RV64GCV CPU contract and saddle us with costly RTL, UCIe package, and physical silicon rework. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are our remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting? | Missing physical checks, red-teaming verification, LLM judge confirmation bias audits, IP indemnification checks, and unverified UCIe power-grid drop block the current tapeout freeze. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** As architects, we choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before our commitment authority decides whether the design advances. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

Ultimately, any claim that we have a feasible system rests on our problem choice, abstractions, and system boundaries. Once we establish those foundations, architecture synthesis allows us to expose missing constraints and cross-layer tradeoffs that isolated specialist results cannot resolve. Our explanation of the underlying mechanisms, coupled with a view of remaining risks, determines whether our recommendation warrants a commitment. In the Lighthouse project, working through these judgments is how we create and synthesize the architecture. We are driving the design.

## Selecting System Abstractions and Bounds {#sec-selecting-abstractions-constraints}

An abstraction represents our technical choice about which details to expose and which to simplify away. We might represent the same design candidate as a CPU instruction mix, an NPU tensor dataflow graph, a cycle-level memory trace model, synthesizable RTL, a 2.5D UCIe chiplet floorplan, or a thermal dissipation model. None of these representations constitute the architecture in isolation. Because each representation highlights specific relationships while suppressing others, we must choose the model whose omissions are safe for the design action under review.

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note on Architecture Description.** ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 distinguishes an entity architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe our chapter organization, our specific design process, or our assignment of authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].
:::

Our choice of abstraction dictates which components contribute to a design decision. As architects, we must ask what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, or tool is allowed to modify and which observations constrain those changes. Simply piling on more components does not guarantee a better composed system. If a component internal simplification obscures a blocking property (such as power delivery network voltage drop or die-to-die thermal coupling), the final result becomes less trustworthy, even if that component boasts local optimizations.

We see this contrast in the AlphaChip macro-placement case [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. An automated macro-placement tool can optimize an NPU accelerator layout locally, but it cannot evaluate whether that placement causes power delivery network (PDN) IR-drop spikes that starve the host CPU or overload the UCIe chiplet thermal dissipator. We define the block boundaries, curate the macro set, establish the timing and power constraints across host CPU and NPU cores, determine the comparison basis, and run the physical signoff checks. Ultimately, we decide whether a given placement serves the chip's goals.

Beyond selecting individual components, we architect how these pieces interact. We decide which architectural state crosses an interface, which downstream component has the authority to revise that state, which independent checks can halt progress, and whether two seemingly distinct verification steps share the same flawed assumptions. The way we arrange this workflow defines which design candidates we can propose and which catastrophic errors might survive our gauntlet.

Often, our most consequential constraints emerge as expert judgment rather than explicitly represented design state. This is *tacit knowledge* (the practical insights that practitioners rely on but cannot always formalize completely) [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]. For instance, our compiler specialist might know that a proposed NPU matrix instruction will lack an efficient lowering path. Similarly, our physical design lead might recognize that a specific placement heuristic is unsafe for our chosen CPU-NPU power-grid geometry.

One application for AI is helping us locate, compare, and organize these scattered expert judgments for formal review. Writing down tacit knowledge does not render it authoritative. Any consequential architectural constraint, assumption, or claim requires a check commensurate with its risk and scope. We might delegate that check to an automated method, a conventional EDA tool, a domain specialist, or an independent peer reviewer. While the domain specialist qualifies the meaning and boundaries of the rule, we must separately decide whether it belongs in the permanent project record. If we accept it, we document its source, its scope, the interfaces it affects, any known conflicts, and the conditions that would prompt us to reopen the decision.

Consider a physical designer who enforces a rule against placing two high-current macros on the same power stripe. The specialist provides the qualifying geometry and safe operating threshold. As architects, we decide how to enforce this. We must evaluate whether the resulting routing overhead serves the larger design goals. If we later change our power-grid template or switch to a 3D stacked die configuration, we invalidate the original basis of the rule. We must then trigger a formal review rather than leaving the obsolete constraint in force as if it were timeless expertise.

We must remember that not every expert intuition should crystallize into a formal rule. While an unrecorded constraint risks being optimized away, an overgeneralized constraint can reject innovative designs. Our responsibility is navigating this tension, deciding whether a piece of knowledge belongs in model state, an environment constraint, a rejection check, or human specialist judgment.

Ultimately, we must compose all of these components, tools, and specialist judgments into a single, coherent architectural system.

## Governing System Integration {#sec-orchestrating-system-integration}

We elevate a design candidate to a true architecture only when its mechanisms and interfaces interoperate across every layer governing product behavior. To do this properly, our recommendation must encompass cross-layer system effects that no single automated optimizer could represent. Our architecture team composes specialist judgments rather than replacing them. Our compiler, verification, physical design, memory, packaging, and product domain experts each establish specialized results within their own scopes. To synthesize a working solution, we must adjust the system across layers. While no such revision was executed in the retained Lighthouse records, this sequence illustrates the process of architecture creation. Our team must preserve this architectural coherence as work naturally disperses among various people, models, and tools. As architects, our synthesis task is to determine whether these disparate results align to form one coherent system decision, and we must constantly hunt for any unexamined interfaces hiding between them.

We make this synthesis concrete by walking through a hypothetical future revision of the Lighthouse XR SoC. Suppose our trace analysis supports the frame rate target, our compiler search finds a legal NPU tiling strategy, our RTL simulation decisively passes, our SRAM model satisfies its local bandwidth checks, and our accelerator block closes timing. Excellent, until we combine the results. We discover that our NPU tiling raises burst memory traffic, pushing the SRAM and UCIe chiplet interconnect beyond our 3\ W thermal limit, while a critical tail latency case lacks software fallback. To synthesize a working solution, we must change the system holistically. We assign tail latency handling to the host CPU core, narrow the NPU accelerator DMA interface, reconfigure our buffering and memory scheduling schemes, and inject a firmware fallback path. If post-silicon validation uncovers an unexpected race condition in the hardware DMA controller, our architecture team must deploy microcode chicken-bits (programmable control register overrides that disable problematic speculative microarchitectural paths) to quarantine the silicon bug without forcing an expensive respin. Our domain specialists jump back in to reassess all affected contracts. While no such drastic revision was executed in the retained Lighthouse records, this sequence illustrates the heart of architecture creation. We iterate on mechanisms, interfaces, and partitioning until our local, specialized results converge into one feasible, unified product.

Crucially, our team must preserve this architectural coherence as work disperses among various people, models, and tools. Candidate identity, baseline assumptions, strict interfaces, localized checks, and stopping conditions cannot disappear as we move between components. As architects, we thread these outputs together, from high-level XR workload behavior down through tensor tiling, interconnect traffic, memory buffering, the rigid 3\ W thermal boundary, and software fallback mechanisms. We produce an actionable recommendation bounded by an explicit scope, detailing both supporting and conflicting results alongside all known limits. While our domain-level checks qualify what our recommendation can support, they do not authorize the final product commitment.

## Resolving Cross-Layer Discrepancies {#sec-resolving-discrepancies}

As we established in @sec-feedback-verification-trust, a check can only support what its scope, uncertainty, and independence justify. Computer architecture introduces complexity when qualified results disagree. A performance result might support a local NPU ranking, yet if we cannot explain the underlying mechanism, we cannot safely transfer that result to a changed workload, host CPU software path, interface, or physical silicon implementation. When faced with this, we must narrow our claim, request a discriminating test, or keep the dependent transition blocked.

We cannot settle these decisions by counting votes. First, our domain experts must determine whether the conflicting checks encode the same contract and conditions. If they do, a blocking failure remains a failure. If they do not, we must correct the architectural abstraction or interface definition, then rerun the affected paths. When our experts cannot reconcile these scopes, we must keep the transition blocked and escalate the unresolved system contract, resisting the urge to choose the more convenient result.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared blocking property between host CPU caches and NPU DMA engine stores, even though our high-level software model treats that execution as legal under high-contention LPDDR5 traffic. We cannot weaken the property, discard the failing workload, or recast the counterexample as a pass. Our technical question must be whether the formal property and the software model encode the identical product contract. If they do, the candidate fails. If they do not, we must correct the underlying architecture problem and rerun both paths. Ultimately, this disagreement exposes a system interface error that no localized score can resolve.

Not every uncertainty halts all progress. Suppose we have two feasible candidates with overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. As architects, we must identify whether workload sampling, model error, or an untested operating corner could reverse our choice. We request the least costly higher-fidelity observation capable of discriminating between them, such as matched cycle-level trace runs, physical thermal simulation, or implementation-facing power-grid analysis. If no available observation can resolve the overlap within our budget, we must keep our recommendation narrow and our choice reversible rather than treating the nominal mean as a mandate.

Ultimately, our interpretation connects each result to a consequence. A timing pass cannot handwave an open power delivery failure or UCIe PHY signal integrity error, just as proving a declared formal property cannot guarantee that the property captured the desired product behavior. We must synthesize these scoped judgments to form a coherent architectural vision.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
While automation may handle local formulation, exploration, implementation, and analysis, our architectural judgment dictates the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries. We must synthesize cross-layer dependencies across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers, interpret conflicting evidence, and forge a supported recommendation. Every design review must identify the ultimate decision maker and trace exactly how isolated results unite to form one feasible system. Without this oversight, even successful tool runs can prop up a flawed architecture.
:::

Any real design commitment demands this integrated account of our architecture problem, the system we are building, and the meaning of our results.

## Separating Evidence from Commitments {#sec-linking-results-claims-commitments}

When we synthesize our technical findings, we produce a comprehensive architecture recommendation rather than a final commitment. In our recommendation, we outline the preferred design alongside alternatives, detail the conditions and checks underpinning our comparisons, and highlight any conflicting data. We set the limits that will govern our next design transition. While we integrate findings into a unified cross-layer technical recommendation, we do not override our specialized peers. Our domain experts in verification, timing closure, physical design, power integrity, packaging, safety, security, and reliability retain responsibility for their respective signoffs.

Our two independent evaluation tests from @sec-moonshot remain intact. We rely on architectural evidence to establish what our design supports, while separately classifying our program claims as supported, unsupported, or unresolved. This status reflects whether we should adopt a specific design methodology, not whether we commit to a particular hardware architecture. Neither test gives us the authority to force a design transition.

Once we have a result, our responsible domain specialists state its validity and scope. As architects, we weave that validated result into our cross-layer technical recommendation. From there, our designated commitment authority decides whether we advance the design, freeze an interface, or proceed to tapeout. The accountable organization must resource the work and own all product consequences. Generating a qualified result, formulating a system recommendation, and executing an authorized decision remain distinct architectural actions that cannot substitute for one another.

The program claim statuses we developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect leave various architectural pathways open. No single status can unilaterally dictate our final design commitment (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program claim status** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| **Supported** | Our repeated, matched comparisons across declared tasks and conditions show that our complete approach clears the decision boundary. We may still refuse the architecture if we find the physical design, supporting evidence, organizational capacity, or residual risk to be unacceptable. |
| **Unsupported** | Our matched comparisons demonstrate that our claimed advantage fails to clear our core decision criterion. Nevertheless, we may still commit to a structurally sound architecture if it is backed by evidence produced through conventional methodologies. |
| **Unresolved** | We find the comparison to be missing, incomplete, or underpowered. We cannot justify an adoption claim. We may only proceed with the architecture if independent design evidence explicitly supports it. |

: **Program claim status and architecture commitment remain independent.** We cannot substitute a favorable result on one for a favorable result on the other in our architectural methodologies. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Our two evaluation tests can diverge. The evidence we gather for adopting a novel program or synthesis workflow cannot settle whether we should commit to a particular hardware architecture. The critical question is determining what type of architectural commitment follows and who owns it.

## Governing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-governing-tapeout-commitments}

When we make an architecture commitment, we make a technical system choice. We are selecting a design and its interfaces for implementation, integration, or release under stated conditions. In our synthesis, we treat reversibility as a design variable. Early in exploration, a commitment is cheap to revise. That flexibility vanishes as our choices harden along the physical commitment curve. We advance from ISA definitions to fixed software interfaces, physical floorplans, UCIe package substrate routings, and mask set generation. Our decision rule is straightforward. We must raise the evidence burden as our design reversals become more costly and irreversible.

Our commitment states what design advances, which alternatives we rejected, which conditions our evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and what would invalidate our choice. We are not certifying that the design is perfect. We establish that our selected system is preferable to alternatives for our stated product obligation, and that we have bounded the remaining uncertainty to justify the next transition.

We must keep three technical decisions separate. Simply running design work does not establish what a result supports, and merely establishing that support does not automatically commit our architecture (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights).

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Our work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Our relevant domain specialists own result validity and domain scope. The architect determines how that result applies to our system decision. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition (e.g., tapeout freeze)? | Our architecture decision composes alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, and residual risk. |

: **Execution, support, and commitment remain distinctly separate technical decisions in our methodology.** When we separate them, we prevent a successful tool run or a favorable local result from silently authorizing our architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

While a classic human-automation framework separates information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation to ask how much of each function we should automate [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation], it provides a useful precedent. It demonstrates the value of separating functions before assigning automation, but it does not fully prescribe our distinction among executing design work, establishing evidentiary support, and committing an architecture.

We cannot let a later judgment rewrite the recorded result of a completed check. Our architecture team can add new results, and changed conditions can render an earlier result inapplicable to our current candidate, but the original outcome remains immutable.

Even though the organizational assignment of these decisions differs across teams, we must never collapse their technical meanings. For example, an design system might perform reversible actions and trigger our declared stops, while our domain specialists establish what those results support. Ultimately, the architect integrates those findings, and our commitment authority decides whether the overarching system advances toward tapeout.

### Residual Risk {#sec-stating-residual-risk}

Committing to an architecture does not mean we have erased every uncertainty. Rather, it means we understand the remaining failure modes well enough to accept, mitigate, or block them. When we grant a bounded exception, we do not change the underlying test result, and a mandatory requirement remains blocking unless we alter the requirement itself. We treat residual risk as an inherent technical property of our decision, not as an administrative label pasted on after the design advances.

Our residual risk statement is usable if a reviewer can connect the failure mode to its consequence, its remaining uncertainty, the detecting check, and our containment or rollback action. We propose these five items as the minimum:

1. **Failure mode.** The explicit architectural, logical, or physical mechanism that could fail.
2. **Consequence.** The impact on performance, power, thermals, data integrity, or safety.
3. **Remaining uncertainty.** The bounds on what is unknown.
4. **Detecting check.** The empirical test, telemetry signal, or monitor assigned to observe the mode.
5. **Containment action.** The verified fallback path, throttling mechanism, or hardware disable fuse.

If we lack a reliable check, operating restriction, or containment path to detect or limit the failure, we must block the design transition entirely.

To test what containment requires, consider a future Lighthouse candidate featuring an optional vector turbo mode on our NPU whose subsystem power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. This mode is not part of our retained Lighthouse evidence. Merely retaining its circuitry for later study would not justify enabling it in production. For us to craft a defensible exception, we would require a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted to an authorized lab mode, and verified reset, fault, and access control behavior. We would also demand proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate our base design requirements, alongside a named owner and a firm expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. If we cannot validate the disabled state, isolation, or restricted enable path, we must remove the feature or halt the design advance toward tapeout. The exception does not transform missing evidence into a passing grade. At expiration, we face a decision point: authorize enablement using new evidence, renew a narrower exception, keep the mode disabled, or remove it.

If we allow repeated exceptions, a known failure morphs into our accepted baseline, triggering the normalization of deviance described by @Vaughan1996Challenger. Enforcing expiration and reopening prevents a temporary decision from becoming permanent because our reporting systems fall silent.

### Hardware Containment {#sec-enforcing-containment}

Our containment authority matters only when our design provides a technical lever. Depending on the failure, that lever might manifest as a verified hardware feature-disable fuse, a safe firmware fallback, a thermal derating mode, redundant physical lanes in a UCIe link, a memory isolation boundary, a rollback path, or our refusal to expose the capability to software. Some physical failures offer no safe containment short of physical repair or replacement. If we lack a credible containment lever, that absence alone provides reason for us to refuse a difficult-to-reverse tapeout commitment.

Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance policies. We must verify the disabled state, isolate the failure from required behavior, and ensure our control path remains available even under the active fault being contained. While errata and later silicon steppings give us channels for describing and repairing post-silicon defects, we know that not every erratum has a workaround, and not every subsequent stepping actually fixes the problem.

### NRE and Tapeout ROI Gatekeeping

Advancing a candidate architecture from software simulation to physical silicon requires committing non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital. We define *NRE tapeout ROI gatekeeping* as the architectural governance process of evaluating whether candidate PPA gains deliver sufficient return on investment to justify committing fixed capital before freezing silicon. As illustrated in @fig-nre-mask-cost-productivity, while design synthesis delivers a scaling curve in front-end design productivity, it does not lower the reticle mask set cost wall. A leading-edge tapeout demands tens of millions of dollars for reticle mask sets, foundry shuttle runs, EDA tool licensing, and physical design teams. The lead architect and commitment authority serve as the ultimate ROI gatekeepers. Before authorizing a tapeout freeze for an RV64GCV core and NPU matrix accelerator, we must verify that an architectural candidate delivers a sufficient return on investment to justify the NRE gate. We weigh expected PPA performance gains across XRBench, SPEC2026, and MLPerf workloads against the financial risk of committing unverified RTL to silicon.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nre-mask-cost-productivity
#| fig-cap: |

As design automation compresses front-end labor, reticle mask costs escalate, shifting the primary capital bottleneck to physical mask fabrication.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Dual-axis line chart plotting reticle mask set NRE costs and front-end engineering design labor costs across process nodes from 90nm to 2nm on log scales. Fixed mask costs escalate from $1.5M to $180M while front-end design costs drop."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

nodes = ["90nm", "45nm", "28nm", "16nm", "7nm", "3nm", "2nm"]

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.86, top=0.86, bottom=0.20)

ax1.set_yscale("log")
l1 = ax1.plot(
    x,

    color=COLORS["blue"],
    linewidth=2.0,
    marker="o",

l2 = ax1.plot(
```

### IP Indemnification and Patent Risk

When integrating generated RTL, Triton kernel passes, or foundation models into a production SoC, architectural governance faces *IP indemnification and patent risk*, defined as the unshielded legal liability an organization assumes when generative models emit microarchitectural structures or HDL snippets that reproduce patented designs without contractual vendor warranty. Commercial IP blocks purchased from established vendors come with contractual indemnification that protects the organization against litigation. In contrast, code emitted by generative models carries no legal warranty. If a model echoes patented microarchitectural structures, proprietary bus protocols, or copyrighted HDL snippets, the organization faces unindemnified legal liability and potential injunctions against shipping the physical silicon. As architects, we must enforce strict IP provenance tracking, static clean-room verification, and legal indemnification checks before committing generated RTL to a tapeout.

### Auditing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-evaluating-lighthouse-commitment}

Our current lack of system boundary, UCIe packaging, and physical implementation evidence supports a recommendation to keep our Lighthouse transition open. This missing data does not prove that our design passes or fails, and it does not authorize a final architecture commitment or tapeout freeze.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
Our prospective cache study did not run, and our separate array result fails to establish the full workload suite, the RV64GCV vector ISA contract, the compiler lowering path, the interconnect energy and memory hierarchy data movement, the 3\ W subsystem thermal boundary, the physical implementation, or the required legal and ROI checks. Consequently, our present technical recommendation is to leave the freeze and tapeout commitment undecided, pending qualified checks of those requirements across all 8 layers of the Lighthouse Prompt Stack. We emphasize that this is a recommendation to continue our technical work. It is neither a finding that the design passes or fails, nor permission to advance the pipeline. We keep these two records separate for later review.
:::

We must ensure that a later review qualifies those missing results before our architect can recommend advancing the design, and before our commitment authority can authorize that tapeout transition. If we wish to make a broader program adoption claim, we must demand matched comparisons of our complete architectural approaches.

## Sustaining Ownership and Responsibility {#sec-sustaining-responsibility}

We must retain the ability to challenge and reopen our architectural decisions across the entire lifecycle. Simply naming an owner does not build this capacity. To maintain control over a design, we must ensure that our design candidates, boundary conditions, rejected alternatives, simulation results, unresolved disagreements, and overall status remain inspectable across CPU, NPU, memory, and UCIe packaging layers. Our architecture teams and domain specialists need access to the tools, testbenches, physical signoff reports, and artifacts capable of exposing a mistake later in the lifecycle.

### Engineering Competence {#sec-preserving-challenge-capacity}

The irony of automation warns us that heavy automation can erode the hands-on practice that developed our technical intuition [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. We are not arguing to keep routine verification manual. We need to test whether our architects and specialists can still inspect tool behavior, analyze failed candidates, and formulate cross-layer diagnoses when the automation falls short.

@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones coined the term *moral crumple zone* to describe a person forced to absorb the blame for an automated system despite lacking meaningful control over its behavior. Naming a reviewer who lacks access to decisive artifacts and the authority to halt a design transition creates an analogous risk. Even with access, we face *automation bias* (the tendency to blindly accept incorrect automated synthesis advice or overlook layout problems our tools failed to flag) [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. While flying a simulator is not direct evidence of how we review chip architectures, these lessons motivate us to test whether our challenge paths work under pressure.

We must demonstrate this challenge capacity through concrete technical work. An architect or domain specialist needs the ability to reproduce or commission selective, decisive checks. We must be able to inspect failed design candidates, diagnose seeded logic or timing faults in host CPU or NPU blocks, and reassess our evidence whenever an underlying EDA tool or architectural parameter changes. For a few exercises, we should require an independent human diagnosis before we look at the automated tool recommendation. Each exercise concludes with our architects recording how their findings alter the baseline recommendation, leaving the commitment authority to decide whether the transition advances, narrows, holds, or reopens. This approach connects our technical competence to the architectural decisions we are challenging.

Opaque external dependencies do not absolve us of responsibility. A black box vendor IP block, a foundry process design kit (PDK), or a commercial EDA tool may restrict what our architecture teams can inspect. When making a tapeout commitment, we must identify the exact IP versions, interface assumptions, available independent cross-checks, and the failure modes that will remain difficult to diagnose. If our observations cannot support the required claim or provide a safe fallback mechanism, moving forward is unsound. A vendor certificate merely establishes provenance. It is never a substitute for an independent technical check.

### Transferring Architectural Basis {#sec-transferring-technical-basis}

Our unresolved Lighthouse project makes this ongoing responsibility concrete. When we hand off that project, the receiving architects need more than a final status update. They require the technical foundation and the conditions that could support a later decision. Any transfer of architectural responsibility must pass along the technical basis, not merely a summary report.

When we defer work, we carry forward the missing obligations that previously prevented a commitment. Similarly, a rejected microarchitectural alternative must retain the basis for its rejection, returning to consideration only if a relevant physical, memory, or workload condition changes.

The successor team must receive the candidate release identity, the design question, and the system boundaries. We must provide them with our baseline assumptions, explored alternatives, and the spectrum of decisive results (passed, failed, inconclusive, and notably missing across CPU, NPU, memory, and UCIe packaging layers). We must outline the remaining uncertainty and detail any validated containment paths. A successful transfer identifies which shifts in workload, software stack, EDA tools, manufacturing process, interface standards, or observed behaviors would render the original decision inapplicable. If proprietary boundaries limit reproduction, the transfer documentation must specify which artifacts only a credentialed domain specialist can inspect.

Whenever one of those critical conditions changes, our architects must initiate a technical reconsideration. We do not expect the new team to personally rerun every regression check. Instead, they ensure the relevant domain specialists reconsider the decision, preventing us from blindly reusing an outdated result. We explore this transfer analysis deeply in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, addressing what artifacts transfer cleanly and which verification work we must repeat.

### Silicon Telemetry {#sec-monitoring-reopening-decisions}

The technical basis we transfer dictates what our monitoring systems must watch. We identify which workload mixes, software and firmware stacks, operating voltage ranges, supplier component versions, tool qualifications, and physical thermal conditions demand observation. Product telemetry exposes architectural shifts through tail latency spikes in CPU task queues, UCIe link retries, LPDDR5 ECC errors, NPU thermal throttling, and recurring reset signatures. These observations only matter if we tie them directly to a boundary condition or a failure mode capable of overturning an architecture decision.

Any reopening trigger must drive a named technical action. A shifting workload or a major software release might force us to requalify our performance and memory hierarchy behavior. When we encounter a new erratum, a supplier revision, or a production failure in deployed systems, we may need to execute a containment action, push a firmware patch, derate the operating frequency, disable a faulty feature, tape out a new stepping, or refuse further deployment. Our specialists pinpoint the affected results, our architects revise the recommendation, and our commitment authority dictates the next transition. Ultimately, our accountable organization owns the product response. System monitoring is the active maintenance of our living architecture decisions.

Observed failures frequently force us to reopen a commitment. While failing silicon proves that a breakdown occurred under observed conditions, it rarely hands us the root cause. Investigations must disentangle whether the fault stems from the workload, software stack, host CPU logic, NPU spatial tiles, UCIe packaging, manufacturing variations, environmental stressors, or operational edge cases.

The Pentium FDIV bug illustrates this reality. @Edelman1997PentiumDivision documents specific lookup table entries that returned 0 instead of 2. While this defect escaped into released silicon, the public account does not reconstruct every internal handoff that allowed the error to slip through. Evidence from systems deployed in the wild invalidated the confidence behind a released processor design. It demanded renewed architecture work, containment strategies, and a decision about how to handle the affected products.

## Ecosystem Outlook for Architecture 2.0 at Scale {#sec-field-level-outlook}

As operational governance practices mature, their cumulative impact extends far beyond single projects. When closed-loop exploration, automated verification, cross-layer optimization, and self-correcting tool orchestration function at scale, the bottlenecks of chip design undergo a structural shift. This transformation reshapes five dimensions of our discipline: architect ownership, EDA industry structures, semiconductor economics, academic curriculum, and global chip innovation.

### Architect Ownership and Skill Transformation

As design loops absorb the mechanics of RTL coding, floorplanning, and place-and-route, the primary contribution of the architect shifts. Upstream, architects focus on formal problem framing, prompt stack specification, objective function synthesis, and safety constraint setting. Downstream, architects govern residual risk, evaluate cross-layer trade-offs, and conduct adversarial red-teaming of recommendations.

The architect becomes a design system architect who engineers both the hardware system and the autonomous loops that build it. Technical contact is preserved by auditing decision traces, inspecting failure counterexamples, and running independent verification checks. The human responsibility remains unchanged: architects must declare what the evidence supports, accept residual risk, and recommend commitments to authorized decision makers.

### EDA Industry Structures and Business Models

The widespread deployment of Architecture 2.0 disrupts traditional EDA market dynamics. Legacy suites built around monolithic, desktop-bound GUI licenses give way to cloud-native, API environments. Conventional EDA tools are repurposed as headless execution tools and verification oracles within agentic loops.

Simultaneously, open-source EDA infrastructures paired with search engines achieve parity with proprietary toolchains for a growing spectrum of SoC blocks. Business models transition from static annual licenses to outcome-contingent pricing, where customers pay based on design space exploration volume or verified PPA closure.

### Semiconductor Economics and Capital Allocation

Architecture 2.0 compresses front-end engineering design cycles from years to weeks and reduces headcount requirements, lowering the NRE cost barrier for initial SoC design. However, it does not reduce fixed back-end capital costs such as reticle mask sets, foundry shuttle runs, and packaging.

Consequently, the economic bottleneck shifts to back-end physical mask fabrication and packaging yield. This shift triggers a surge in domain-specific ASICs. Custom chips for micro-verticals become economically viable at low volumes, ending the era of monolithic general-purpose silicon dominance.

### Academic Curriculum and Pedagogical Transformation

Computer architecture education must undergo a revolution. Teaching students to manually write HDL or hand-craft pipeline units as the measure of competence is obsolete. Curricula must pivot toward four areas:

- Formal specification and multi-layer prompt stack engineering.
- Autonomous verification harness design and red-teaming methodologies.
- Evaluator-driven search space formulation and Pareto trade-off synthesis.
- System integration across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging boundaries.

To prevent students from becoming moral crumple zones, pedagogy must incorporate diagnostic labs. Students must debug seeded cross-layer failures in synthesized microarchitectures, building physical intuition and diagnostic competence without getting bogged down in routine manual implementation.

### Global Chip Innovation and Ecosystem Dynamics

The combination of design loops, open ISAs (RISC-V), open chiplet interconnect standards (UCIe), and cloud compute democratizes custom silicon creation. Hardware startups, regional research centers, and small academic laboratories gain the capability to design competitive, high-performance SoCs previously reserved for mega-cap firms.

Furthermore, hardware development cadences align with agile software release cycles. Silicon architectures iterate on quarterly or monthly schedules using modular chiplet updates and rapid automated design passes, accelerating global hardware innovation.

## Common Pitfalls {#sec-ownership-pitfalls}

As we shift our methodologies, we introduce operational and governance risks when delegating technical work. Automation cannot absorb our accountability for cross-layer synthesis or the ultimate product consequences. To maintain ownership, we must navigate a spectrum of failure modes:

- **Manual HDL Lock-In:** Dismissing architectural tools as unproven and clinging to manual HDL workflows. Conservative organizations that refuse to integrate generative search, fast surrogate evaluation, and automated verification loops forfeit NRE cost efficiency and schedule advantages, rendering their teams obsolete.
- **Conflating EDA Execution with Tapeout Authority:** Assuming that because an agent can execute a complex EDA flow or synthesize a novel microarchitecture, it possesses the authority to commit that design to silicon. Technical execution remains within a bounded evaluator, whereas commitment requires human architects to synthesize cross-layer tradeoffs across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers while shouldering residual risk. We must never allow a green EDA exit code to authorize signoff without expert review.
- **Unverified Black-Box IP Signoff:** Accepting third-party models, vendor IP blocks, or generated chiplet configurations without interrogating their interface invariants. If we cannot trace a multi-layer failure through an opaque component, or if we lack independent verification checkers, we have surrendered our technical contact and can no longer guarantee system coherence.
- **Normalization of Deviance in Synthesis Workarounds:** Repeatedly approving automated workarounds or constraint relaxations (such as disabling a hardware feature or stretching a thermal design envelope) to force timing or placement closure. Accepting these synthetic exceptions without enforcing containment paths, hard expiration conditions, and post-silicon validation normalizes deviance, converting temporary technical debt into permanent architectural vulnerability.
- **Autonomous Tapeout Signoff:** Relinquishing cross-layer architect ownership and delegating silicon tapeout signoff to automated models without human governance, empirical proof of correctness, or residual risk auditing. Complete surrender turns engineering leaders into moral crumple zones who inherit liability for catastrophic post-silicon bugs, thermal runaways, or multi-million-dollar mask re-spins while having abandoned the diagnostic contact required to prevent them.

## Open Questions {#sec-ownership-open-questions}

As synthesis tools absorb the mechanics of design generation and verification, our intellectual focus must shift. We must compose, interrogate, and govern the systems we build. Resolving these challenges demands inquiry and experimentation.

### Architectural Judgment and Technical Competence {#sec-rq-judgment}

- **Evaluating Challenge Capacity.** How can we quantitatively measure whether an engineering team retains the capacity to audit, challenge, and veto an agent-synthesized microarchitecture before tapeout?
- **Pedagogical Interventions.** What educational frameworks and diagnostic benchmarks prevent automation bias and the irony of automation among architects?

### EDA Tool Architectures and Agentic Infrastructure {#sec-rq-eda-infrastructure}

- **Decoupled Execution and Verification.** How should next-generation EDA infrastructures decouple generative synthesis agents from formal verification oracles to prevent confirmation bias and hallucination?
- **Open-Source Evaluator Ecosystems.** Can open-source EDA tools provide sufficient fidelity as evaluation oracles to drive exploration loops without requiring proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) exposure?

### Semiconductor Economics and NRE Governance {#sec-rq-economics}

- **Quantifying NRE ROI Gates.** What algorithmic metrics evaluate whether an AI-proposed microarchitectural optimization justifies the fixed multi-million-dollar NRE mask cost of a leading-edge tapeout?
- **IP Provenance and Automated Indemnification.** What static analysis and provenance-tracing algorithms can guarantee that generated HDL snippets do not infringe on proprietary patent portfolios?

### System Boundary Visibility and Cross-Layer Telemetry {#sec-rq-telemetry}

- **Cross-Layer Failure Diagnosis.** What diagnostic telemetry interfaces must be built into 2.5D/3D chiplet packages to isolate runtime failures between host CPUs, NPU tensor arrays, and UCIe PHY links?
- **Bounded Abstractions for Opaque IP.** What observable interface invariants allow architects to safely integrate third-party black-box IP into search loops without losing system-level correctness guarantees?

### Global Chip Innovation and Agile Hardware Cadences {#sec-rq-agile-hardware}

- **Continuous Chip Integration.** How can hardware organizations synchronize automated silicon synthesis loops with rapid software release cycles without compromising tapeout reliability?
- **Democratized Hardware Benchmarks.** What versioned benchmark infrastructures can objectively evaluate design loops across global research organizations?

## Conclusion {#sec-closing-moonshot-coda}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate technical work, not architectural accountability"}
While we can delegate technical execution, a named, technically qualified, and institutionally empowered authority must retain the power to stop, commit, or reopen any architecture decision. Our accountable organization must own the downstream consequences and provide resources for monitoring and recovery. As commitment authorities, we must inspect the technical basis, maintaining a separation between a recommendation and a final commitment. We consider a review to have failed this principle if the assigned owner cannot inspect decisive evidence, block a transition, or secure resources to respond to post-commitment failures.
:::

We close this book without a definitive Lighthouse verdict. As we recorded in @sec-running-the-loop, our prospective cache study did not run. Furthermore, the array study supports only a localized no-change finding for the specific array shapes we evaluated. It supplies zero evidence for the full system, our 3\ W subsystem target, or the pinned physical implementation. We recorded no final architecture commitment.

Providing these missing checks and matched comparisons is the work we are asking the machine learning and computer architecture communities to take up. To build a credible architectural benchmark, we require a versioned workload, software stack, and reference design. We must define a clear action space and constraints; deliver executable tool and evidence tracks; and establish evaluator-owned checks and metrics. We need matched conventional and no-added-assistance baselines backed by total cost accounting. We demand retained provenance, rigorous contamination controls, clear task splits, and durable governance for maintenance and versioning. The XR Lighthouse Request supplies our core design question and outlines these exact requirements. Building the versioned artifacts, executable tracks, and governance structures to realize this benchmark is the grand challenge we present.

In taking up this challenge, we preserve our two independent tests. First, our matched comparisons must conclusively establish whether the complete design system improves architecture quality, lowers total cost, or both, when compared to a credible alternative. Even if we can support that program claim, we must separately integrate the technical evidence and recommend whether the selected design and its residual risks justify commitment. A named commitment authority must make the final call on whether the architecture advances to tapeout. If our assessment finds no clear adoption advantage, we might still advance the same architecture through a conventional workflow. We must recognize that a component-level AI contribution remains unresolved when controlled replacement or ablation cannot isolate it from broader system interactions. We cannot let the absence of a verdict masquerade as a success claim.

Our discipline needs durable cross-layer abstractions that connect workload and software behavior down to microarchitecture, host CPUs, NPU tensor engines, memory systems, UCIe chiplet interconnects, and physical silicon implementation. We require interfaces that expose assumptions and uncertainty to our tools and reviewers, alongside system-wide evaluations that compare complete architectural approaches rather than isolated model outputs. Architecture 2.0 requires us to engineer and leverage design systems while owning the architecture problem, the cross-layer synthesis, the technical recommendation, and its continued validity. While automation extends the scale of technical work we can attempt, it is ultimately up to us as architects to decide whether the resulting mechanisms and interfaces form a coherent system. We make the recommendation on what should be built. A commitment authority decides whether the system advances to silicon. Our accountable organization remains answerable for the real-world consequences. We must be ready to reopen our technical recommendations the moment workloads, software, tools, process conditions, or observed silicon behaviors shift. It is this continuing technical oversight that elevates automation into true computer architecture.
